title: Hyperscaler managed endpoints opportunity map and pitch fragments
body:
Purpose:
A compact, tactical reference for AE/SE teams to map commercial/technical opportunity vs AWS/GCP/Azure managed endpoint offerings and to surface fast pitch fragments and objections-to-rebuttals for live deals. This is intentionally pragmatic — prioritized playbook items, short scripts, and migration friction signals.

Audience:
- Field AEs and Solutions Engineers
- Growth SDRs qualifying for technical buyers
- Product marketing for messaging checks

Executive summary (2 lines):
- Hyperscalers win with integrated cloud convenience but lose on predictable per-token economics, inference-specific ops, and developer ergonomics for production LLM workloads.
- Redwood’s angle: move buyers from “easy to start” to “costly to scale” — emphasize predictable latency, cost controls, private deployment, and operational fallbacks.

Opportunity map (how we win by buyer type):
- AI-native startups: prioritize predictable cost per inference + low latency. Pitch: "same API surface, 3–5x lower unit cost at scale with safe fallbacks".
- Mid-market product teams: care about compliance and SLAs; pitch private deployment + dedicated pooling + audit logs.
- Platform teams: need homogeneous runtime across clouds and on-prem; pitch unified operator experience + rollout controls + model pinning.

Migration friction matrix (signals we win quickly):
- Procurement friction: High for enterprise because hyperscaler contracts are broad; signal: RFP for "inference SLAs".
- Data residency/compliance: High for healthcare/finance; signal: request for VPC/private/public cloud separation.
- Cost surprise: Hyperscaler customers often flag unpredictable token spend and autoscaling bills; signal: teams asking for "cost projections by QPS".
- Latency SLOs: teams with 99th percentile latency targets; signal: mention of "sub-200ms first token" or real-time chat.
- Ops maturity: If they have a platform org or central ML infra, they prefer control; signal: "we’re standardizing on a single inference runtime".

Top technical win themes (short, actionable):
- Predictable per-token economics: show a small model economics spreadsheet — units, batching, cache hit assumptions. Offer a calc during POC.
- Smart fallback and routing: show how Redwood routes by cost/latency and auto-falls back to quantized variants without client changes.
- Unified interface across modes: hosted API for devs -> Dedicated for scale -> Private for regs; same SDK and rollout knobs. This reduces integration debt.
- Operational primitives that matter: KV/prefix cache, continuous batching, model rollouts, token-level tracing. Hyperscalers offer endpoints but not inference-first ops at this granularity.

Sample objection / rebuttal pairs (copyable):
- Objection: "We already run on Vertex/Azure — we don’t want vendor sprawl."
  Rebuttal: "Totally fair. Redwood is a drop-in inference layer — same REST/SDK patterns. Most customers keep their cloud contracts and use Redwood for predictable inference economics, model rollouts, and private deployment where needed. We can work with your cloud account or run in your VPC."

- Objection: "Hyperscaler endpoints give us the whole stack and billing simplicity."
  Rebuttal: "They do for general compute. For LLMs, teams tell us they get predictable convenience but unpredictable monthly bills. We show a POC that projects per-token spend under realistic QPS and caching assumptions and put autoscaling/burst controls in the SOW to avoid surprises."

- Objection: "We care about model access/features like multimodal or managed fine-tuning on the hyperscaler."
  Rebuttal: "Redwood partners with model providers and maintains a curated catalog with verified performance profiles; for advanced model features we map the compatibility surface and provide a migration path — often with Dedicated or Private deployments for model variants."

Competitive notes (concise, distinct bullets per hyperscaler):
- AWS SageMaker / Bedrock style endpoints:
  - Strengths: deep integration into AWS infra, IAM/KMS, marketplace model options, single-bill convenience.
  - Weaknesses: endpoint-per-model scaling, coarse-grained batching, limited inference-first primitives, unit-cost opacity at scale.
  - Redwood counter: highlight autoscaling controls, continuous batching efficiency, and explicit quantization recommendations for predictable unit economics.

- GCP Vertex AI endpoints:
  - Strengths: good developer tooling for MLOps, strong data/BigQuery integrations.
  - Weaknesses: latency variability under bursty traffic, less emphasis on token-level tracing, rollout primitives are not inference-specific.
  - Redwood counter: offer tracing and per-route dashboards + model rollout controls tailored for production LLMs.

- Azure Managed/OpenAI endpoints:
  - Strengths: enterprise security posture, single-bill for MS customers, Azure AD integrations.
  - Weaknesses: closed model feature dependency (for OpenAI flavors), limited GPU granularity for dedicated inference, per-request cost unpredictability.
  - Redwood counter: private deployment with enterprise KMS/HSM, dedicated GPU pools and predictable throughput SLAs; native AAD integrations possible via Private control plane.

Pricing/contract angle (how to frame it quickly):
- Lead with unit economics language: "We’ll show you a 12-week projection: cost/token, cache-hit assumptions, and autoscaling buffers."
- Offer reserved capacity + burst overlay for Dedicated as a bridge from hyperscaler pay-as-you-go to predictability.
- For POCs, propose a short fixed-fee pilot that includes ingestion of 2–3 production routes and a clear success metric (QPS, 99P latency, and cost per 1M tokens).

Quick SE prep checklist (what to run in a demo/POC):
- Collect sample traffic distribution (avg seq len, peak QPS, % repeated prefixes).
- Run a micro-benchmark: first-token latency, throughput at target batch sizes, and cost projection with caching enabled.
- Show a live rollout: promote a quantized model variant and demonstrate automatic fallback to a higher-quality model under load.
- Bring a sample bill projection matching their cloud region and instance/sku preferences.

One-page battle-card snippets (soundbites for reps):
- "If cost is the worry: we convert your hypothesis into a 12-week projected burn and cost-per-token target you can sign off on."
- "If latency is the worry: we guarantee predictable 99P latency through dedicated pools and knobbed batching policies."
- "If compliance is the worry: we run in your VPC/on-prem with KMS/HSM integration and audit logs the security team can ingest."

Operational risks and mitigation (for AE->CS handoff):
- Risk: underestimated traffic patterns cause cost overages. Mitigation: include autoscale caps and cost-guard rails in deployment plan.
- Risk: model behavior regression post-migration. Mitigation: tie rollout to evals/prompt tests and enable metric-based automatic rollback.
- Risk: integration drift between dev and prod. Mitigation: document identical SDK calls and provide migration guide + runbook.

Open questions we should answer before finalizing pitch pack:
- Do we have up-to-date perf/sla data for the top 3 model families vs the hyperscaler regions they care about?
- Can we produce a templated 12-week cost projection workbook for common workload archetypes (chat, summarization, embeddings)?
- What legal hooks do we need to accelerate Dedicated contracts for mid-market accounts?

Next steps (prioritized):
1) Create a short slide with the migration friction matrix + three customer success stories showing cost/latency wins (owner: Jonah).
2) Build a templated 12-week cost projection workbook and an SE playbook (owner: Priya).
3) Draft an SE demo script that highlights a live rollback and routing policy (owner: Samir).

Notes to self / scratch bits (raw):
- Example POC success metric: reduce 95P latency by 30% while holding cost per 1M tokens within +/-10% of projection.
- Watch for customers saying "we want all-in-one management in Azure" -> emphasize private control plane option.
- Link to internal perf repo for microbenchmarks (TBD).

End.
